background.definition: Acute polyarticular arthritis is pain and inflammation in more than four joints for less than 6 weeks. Chronic arthritis is characterized by symptoms that last longer than 6 weeks.

In 2003, Americans spent a total of $80.8 billion on arthritis medical care.

Osteoarthritis (OA): Exact etiology is unknown. Contributing factors include age, heredity, obesity, and joint injury.
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): No clear evidence to suggest particular cause. Monozygotic twin concordance rate is 12% to 15%.
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS): Highly associated with HLA-B27. Twin concordance rate is less than 60%.
Psoriatic arthritis (PsA): Relative risk is 39 for first-degree relatives. Associated with scalp lesions, nail dystrophy, and gluteal/perineal lesions in psoriasis.
IBD-S: 50% of cases of spondylosis and sacroiliitis are associated with HLA-B27.
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR): Etiology is unknown.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Monozygotic twin concordance rate is 24%. Associated with MHC, HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3. C4a deficiency and C1q deficiency seen in 80% and 90% of patients with SLE, respectively.
Fibromyalgia: Unknown etiology. Associated with depression, chronic headaches, complex regional pain syndrome, nocturnal myoclonus, and irritable bladder.
Osteoarthritis (OA): Degeneration of articular surfaces.
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): An inflammatory cascade produces an invasive synovial tissue pannus that destroys cartilage and bone and leads to the development of systemic complications.
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and IBD-S: Inflammation at the bone/tendon/ligament junction.
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR): Inflammatory cascade creates a systemic inflammatory response.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Autoantibodies form and lead to generalized inflammation, vasculitis, and immune complex deposition.
Fibromyalgia: Unclear pathophysiology.

list.listitem: OA: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) diagnostic criteria published for hand, hip, and knee osteoarthritis.
PMR: Use Bird/Wood criteria.
SLE: ACR diagnostic criteria are available in interactive form.
RA: Diagnostic criteria are available in interactive form.

The initial distinction is inflammatory versus noninflammatory arthritis. Inflammatory arthritides classically have soft-tissue swelling, erythema, and joint effusions, and worsen following immobility. OA: Classic presentation is chronic arthritis with absence of synovitis. Patients are usually older than 50 years with a history of immobilization, joint injury, joint instability, obesity, or occupational stress to the joints. Use ACR criteria.
RA: Suspect RA in patients with painful or swollen MCPs, PIPs, or wrist joints for more than 3 weeks. Symptoms must be present for 6 weeks for a clear diagnosis. Check for prolonged morning stiffness, define the number and distribution of joints involved, and determine the presence of rheumatoid nodules. Patient may also develop constitutional symptoms of fatigue, anorexia, and weakness. RA: If 4 or more of the 7 ACR criteria are present for at least 6 weeks, a diagnosis of RA can be made. If 3 or fewer of the 7 ACR criteria are present, the Netherlands RA clinical prediction score can be used to establish risk for RA development within the next year. RA: In 300 patients with ACR criteria for RA, rapid onset was demonstrated in 46%. Approximately 20% of patients with early RA had no morning stiffness, while approximately 50% presented with more than 1 hour of morning stiffness. AS: Patients present with insidious onset of dull back pain, with pain radiating into gluteal region. Back pain is worse in the morning, improves with activity, and is present at night. May also involve constitutional symptoms. PsA: Pauciarticular (2-4 joints involved) pain in 70% of cases. Usually asymmetric distal joint involvement. Skin symptoms precede joint involvement in 80% of cases. Severity of arthritis does not correlate with cutaneous involvement. Nail involvement, including onycholysis and pitting, is seen in 80% of cases. IBD-S: Abrupt onset, migratory in nature, resolves in 6 to 8 weeks. Typically asymmetric and involves lower extremities. Joint exacerbations tend to coincide with IBD exacerbations. Extra-articular manifestations include bilateral uveitis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum. PMR: Classical presentation is in a patient older than 50 years, with aching pain and morning stiffness involving proximal joints and systemic inflammation. Use Bird/Wood criteria. SLE: Patients may present with constitutional, skin, musculoskeletal, or hematologic symptoms. Arthritis component required to involve two or more peripheral joints with features of synovitis. The ACR diagnostic criteria are less accurate in patients with mild disease. Fibromyalgia: ACR criteria include widespread pain for at least 3 months and 11 of 18 specific tender points positive (tender to palpation). Fibromyalgia impact questionnaire is useful to assess impact on activities of daily living. Subjective swollen joint feeling without objective swelling and paresthesias without objective neurologic findings are two important features of fibromyalgia.

Joint aspiration is reasonable to determine the presence or absence of synovitis. Presence of greater than 2000 WBC/mm3 is considered diagnostic of inflammation. OA: Diagnosis can often be made by history and physical alone, but radiologic findings are useful in ruling out other causes or concurrent processes. RA: The ACR recommends that baseline laboratory evaluations include a CBC with differential, rheumatoid factor, and ESR or CRP. Baseline renal or hepatic function is also recommended to guide therapy. Anti-CCP antibodies are more specific for RA than rheumatoid factor: 95% vs 85%. AS: Radiographic features include bilateral sacroiliitis, with initial sclerosis progressing to erosive changes and total ankylosis or fusion of the sacroiliac joints. Spinal involvement includes enthesitis seen by squaring of the vertebral bodies, and progresses to ossification of the annulus fibrosis that may result in the classic "bamboo spine." Testing for HLA-B27 is not useful in diagnosis. ESR and CRP do not correlate with disease activity. PsA: Radiographic evidence includes erosive arthritis, DIP involvement, enthesitis with periosteal reactions, sacroiliitis, and spondylitis. IBD-S: Anemia is common because of chronic inflammation and blood loss. ESR and CRP levels are elevated. RF and antinuclear antibodies are usually negative. PMR: The Bird/Wood 1979 criteria are still the most sensitive criteria for PMR. The ESR is usually markedly elevated. Normochromic, normocytic anemia, reactive thrombocytopenia, microscopic hematuria, and mild elevations of liver enzymes are common. SLE: ACR criteria have a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 96%. Antinuclear antibody titers have a sensitivity of 98%, but lack specificity. Antinuclear antibody titers are recommended in patients with two or more of the diagnostic criteria, as a persistently negative titer can rule out SLE. Fibromyalgia: No diagnostic testing is directly applicable. Consider testing to determine if other possible etiologies are involved.
A clinical rule to screen for fibromyalgia has been developed and validated.

feature.caption: Suggested Confirmatory Testing for Polyarticular Arthritis.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnosis Confirmatory Tests
Osteoarthritis ACR criteria. Plain films
Rheumatoid arthritis ACR Criteria. Plain film, RF, and anti-CCP
Ankylosing spondylitis Plain films. MRI. RF and ANA for exclusion
Psoriatic arthritis CASPAR criteria. Plain film. RF for exclusion
Inflammatory bowel disease–associated spondyloarthropathy Clinical diagnosis. ESR. RF and ANA for exclusion
Polymyalgia rheumatica Bird/Wood criteria. ESR
Systemic lupus erythematosus ACR criteria. ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith
Fibromyalgia ACR criteria. Clinical diagnosis
ACR, American College of Rheumatology; RF, rheumatoid factor; anti-CCP, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; ESR, erythrocyte sedimentation rate; ANA, antinuclear antibody test.
